blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

blocks.en: 1. Introduction
blocks.zh: 1. 联合国 导言

blocks.en:
Legal education tests a skill that is hard to measure: applying the law
to facts in writing. A German student receives a fact pattern
( Sachverhalt ) and writes an opinion in appraisal style
( Gutachtenstil ); a US student spots the issues in a hypothetical
and argues them; a bar candidate drafts a memo or a judgment. A German
exam case is a proxy for a real case: the fact pattern stands in for the
file a lawyer or a court receives, and the opinion rehearses the
analysis that precedes advice or a decision. These answers run to many
pages, admit more than one defensible solution, and are graded by
experts who often disagree. The same German exam can receive grades
several points apart on the 18-point scale ( Hufeld, 2024 ) , and a
single US law professor’s grade on an essay reached an intraclass
correlation (ICC) of .58 with colleagues ( Klein and Hart, 1968 ) .
Grading is also slow, so students get little feedback before the exam
that counts, although individual feedback measurably improves their
grades ( Schwarcz and Farganis, 2017 ) .

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) have changed both sides of this problem.
They write answers that pass law exams ( Choi et al., 2022 ; Katz et al., 2024 ; Martínez, 2025 ) , so
legal AI needs benchmarks that grade open text. And they offer to grade
answers themselves, as an LLM judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . Since 2025, legal benchmarks and
teaching tools have converged on one design: an expert writes a rubric
for each task, and an LLM checks an answer against it ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Drozdov et al., 2026 ; Al Zubaer et al., 2026 ; Cope et al., 2026 ) .
At the same time, LLM judges are known to drift between runs ( Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025 ) , to favour long answers ( Saito et al., 2023 ) , and to obey instructions embedded in the
answer they grade ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Examination law, data
protection law and the EU AI Act set further limits on what a machine
may decide about a candidate ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2019 ; Court of Justice of the European Union, 2023 ; European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024 ) .

blocks.en:
The literature on these questions is scattered across law reviews,
educational measurement, natural language processing (NLP) and court
decisions. This paper brings them together. Our starting point is that
grading an open-text legal answer is not the prediction of a human grade
but the application of standards that must be stated and justified to
answers that may legitimately differ. Three questions follow: what the
grade should measure, how that performance is translated into criteria
and points, and who answers for that translation and can correct it in
the single case. In short: which way of evaluating open-text legal
answers is best supported by the evidence, for which use, and what must
still be shown before it can be trusted?

blocks.en:
The evidence supports task-specific grading information, above all an
analytic rubric written for the task, as the strongest lever for
agreement with human graders, but no architecture is superior on every
axis: pairwise comparison ordered constructed quality levels better than
rubric scores ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , closed formats are more
reliable, and no rubric judge is yet robust to manipulation. We argue
that rubric-centred grading should nonetheless be the default for
auditable legal assessment. Grading is auditable when the standard, its
application to each script and the final decision can each be checked; a
rubric externalizes the standard, makes each criterion application
contestable and leaves the decision with the examiner. These are design
advantages motivated by examination law, not a claim that the law
mandates one scoring architecture. We therefore propose the trustworthy rubric judge , a rubric judge wrapped in seven
safeguards, and we state the tests it must pass before it grades exams
that count. A companion study, in preparation, builds this judge for
German law exams: it generates the grading sheet from the case and the
reference solution and tests the sheet, the judge and the workflow
against an examiner’s own sheet and grades ( Nagl et al., 2026a ) (Section 10 ).

2. Background: open-text legal answers and how humans grade
them

blocks.en:
The tasks. We call an answer open-text when the candidate
writes free prose that applies law to facts and no answer key can list
every acceptable text. In Germany the core format is the case solution
( Falllösung ): an opinion that states each question, defines the
legal requirements, subsumes the facts and reaches a result, graded on
the statutory scale from 0 to 18 points ( Bundesministerium der Justiz, 1981 ) .
Practice tasks include memos, contract drafting and research answers ( Schwarcz et al., 2026 ; Drozdov et al., 2026 ) and draft
judgments ( Karp et al., 2025 ) . Our core case is the exam; the other
tasks differ in the performance measured as well as in who sets the
standard and what is at stake, so we treat the transfer as a separate
question (Section 10 ).

blocks.en:
Human graders disagree. In a 1968 study, 17 law professors graded
the same 80 contracts essays from 16 schools; a single professor’s grade
reached an intraclass correlation of .58, the mean over all professors
.96, so single graders and panel means are different yardsticks ( Klein and Hart, 1968 ) . On 15 scripts of a German beginner-level mock
exam, each graded by 15 or 16 correctors, the highest and lowest grade
for a script lay 6.47 points apart on average ( Hufeld, 2024 ) , and in
BenGER, a benchmark of German case solutions curated on an open platform ( Nagl and Grabmair, 2026 ) , three blind reviewers reached a single-rater
ICC(2,1) of .63 ( Nagl et al., 2026b ) . Grades in the German state
exams also differ by gender and by the origin of a candidate’s name ( Towfigh et al., 2014 ; Towfigh et al., 2018 ) , and by the Land in which the exam is taken ( Kähler et al., 2017 ) . Grades
rise with length ( Augustine-Adams et al., 2016 ) , legible handwriting ( Greifeneder et al., 2010 ) and legal jargon ( Linn et al., 1972 ) ,
and graders are drawn towards a grade they have already seen ( Vidal Rodeiro, 2007 ; Attali, 2011 ) . Where such
features are not part of what the task tests, this is
construct-irrelevant variance ( Messick, 1995 ) .

blocks.en:
Structure helps, but not alone. An analytic rubric breaks the
expected answer into criteria, each with points or levels; it is instance-specific when it is written for one task rather than for
a type of task ( Dawson, 2017 ) . Rubrics raise agreement
between human raters, especially when they are analytic and
task-specific and come with exemplars or rater training ( Jonsson and Svingby, 2007 ) , and rubrics used formatively improve student
performance with an effect of g g = .45 ( Panadero et al., 2023 ) .
In German law, some correctors note what each part of the expected
solution is worth ( Frenzel, 2011 ) , and a few make this
binding in a grading sheet ( Bewertungsbogen ), described for
take-home papers ( Heidebach, 2015 ) , which narrows the spread
between correctors (Table 3 ). Yet rubrics do not remove
rater effects: raters still differ in severity ( Woitschach et al., 2018 ; Engelhard, 1994 ) , read the same
criteria differently ( Bloxham et al., 2016 ) , and without moderation
shared criteria did not make law marking consistent ( Hanlon et al., 2004 ) . High-stakes testing therefore surrounds the
rubric with machinery: calibration on common scripts, hidden scripts
with known scores to catch drifting severity ( Olson, 2019 ; Congdon and McQueen, 2000 ) , independent double grading
and adjudication ( Light et al., 2024 ) , which the US NextGen bar exam
now adopts for its written answers ( Light et al., 2024 ; Bok and Wesenberg, 2024 ; National Conference of Bar Examiners, 2026 ) .

blocks.en: 3. Method of this systematization
blocks.zh: 3个 系统化方法

blocks.en:
Scope. We draw on three bodies of sources and keep them apart in
the text, since they carry different weight. Direct evidence is work
that grades or evaluates open-text answers to legal tasks, by humans or
machines. Transferred evidence is work from other domains that tests
rubric-based LLM grading against human graders, and the measurement
literature on rubrics and raters. Normative sources are the legal rules
that govern grading: German examination law as the worked example, the
EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and AI Act, and US cases on
academic judgment. We exclude closed formats except where compared with
open text, and supervised essay-scoring models, for which we found no
use on law exams.

German examination law. Exams that control access to a profession
fall under the freedom of occupation (Art. 12(1) of the Basic Law, GG).
Examiners have a margin of appreciation. Each examiner sets their own
standards for a task and must apply them to every script of that task
alike Bundesverfassungsgericht, 1991b , p. 52 ; Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2018 , para.
8 ; the law does not demand one scheme shared by
all examiners. Courts check in full whether a defensible answer was
marked wrong; examination-specific judgments of persuasiveness,
structure and consistency are reviewed only for the limits of that
discretion, a complete and correct reading of the script, equal
application of the examiner’s standards, and freedom from improper
considerations and contradictions ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2018 , paras. 9 to
11) . The candidate has an answer latitude ( Antwortspielraum ): a solution that is defensible
( vertretbar ) and argued consistently with weighty reasons must
not be marked as wrong Bundesverfassungsgericht, 1991a , p. 79 ; Bundesverfassungsgericht, 1991b , p. 55 .
Latitude protects the result, not the mark: a defensible but weakly
argued solution may earn fewer points than a stronger one. An error must
also not be counted twice. A follow-on error ( Folgefehler ) is
reasoning that is wrong or open to criticism only because the candidate
took an earlier decision on the path of the solution, and penalizing it
again is an impermissible double counting ( Doppelverwertung ) ( Verwaltungsgericht Braunschweig, 2018 ) ; how much a follow-on error still weighs is
left to the examiner’s judgment ( Verwaltungsgericht Lüneburg, 2024 ) . The candidate
is owed the essential reasons for the grade ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2019 , para.
23) , though not margin notes that show the reason
for every point, and a point scheme is an aid the examiner may depart
from, not a binding rule ( Bundesfinanzhof, 2014 ) . On substantiated
objections the examiners themselves must reconsider their evaluation; no
other body may do it for them, and written reasons do not replace this
reconsideration ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2019 ) . The examiner must personally
and directly acquaint themselves with each script and evaluate it
independently; an open second correction, in which the second examiner
sees the first grade, is not forbidden by federal constitutional law ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2002 ) .

Data protection. A candidate’s answers and the examiner’s
comments on them are personal data ( Court of Justice of the European Union, 2017 ) , so sending
scripts to a model provider needs a legal basis and a processing
contract. Art. 22 GDPR gives a person the right not to be subject to a
decision based solely on automated processing that has legal or
similarly significant effects, unless the decision is necessary for a
contract, authorized by Union or Member State law with suitable
safeguards, or based on explicit consent ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ) . The Court of
Justice has held that a score is itself such a decision when a third
party’s decision draws strongly on it ( Court of Justice of the European Union, 2023 ) , so an
examiner who adopts a model grade as given risks a solely automated
decision; human involvement must be meaningful ( Colonna, 2024 ) , and the person may require an explanation
of the procedure and principles actually applied ( Court of Justice of the European Union, 2025 ) .

blocks.en: 5. Eight evaluation paradigms

blocks.en:
We distinguish eight paradigms by who grades (human or model) and what
the grade is anchored to (nothing, a reference answer, general criteria,
criteria written for the task, or another answer). They are the
configurations found in the literature, not disjoint classes: the design
space behind them has at least four axes (who grades, what information
the grader receives, whether the judgment is absolute or comparative,
and how partial judgments are aggregated), and real systems mix them, as
a pairwise judge with a rubric does ( Cope et al., 2026 ) . Table 2 rates each paradigm on the desiderata.

blocks.en:
P1 Unstructured human grading (“vibe grading”). An expert reads
the answer and gives a grade, perhaps with margin comments. It is the
legal default and the reference most studies validate against, and an
expert can recognize a defensible alternative that no key foresaw. But
single-rater reliability is moderate, at intraclass correlations of .58
and .63 ( Klein and Hart, 1968 ; Nagl et al., 2026b ) , correctors’ grades
spread widely ( Hufeld, 2024 ) , and length, handwriting, identity and
prior grades leak into the grade (Section 2 ).
blocks.zh:
P1 非结构化的人类分级(“虚拟分级”)。 专家说
回答并给出一个等级,也许附有差值评论。 这是
法定违约和大多数研究所证实的参考文献
专家可以识别出一个没有钥匙预想的可防的替代品。 不过
单发率可靠性中等,等级内关联度为.58
和.63 (Klein and Hart, 1968;Nagl等人, 2026年b), 校正级
(Hufeld,2024年),以及长度、笔迹、身份和
先前的年级漏入年级(第2节)。

blocks.en:
P2 Human grading with an analytic rubric. A rubric makes the
standard explicit, cuts the spread between human graders ( Strecker et al., 2026 ; Jonsson and Svingby, 2007 ) and gives students criteria to
learn from ( Panadero et al., 2023 ; Sparrow, 2004 ) . Its
weaknesses are cost and the remaining rater effects, and it credits
alternatives only if the rubric lists them or the grader departs from
it.
blocks.zh:
P2 带有分析题材的人类分级. 一个数字
(Strecker等人,2026年;Jonsson和Svingby,2007年)。
学习(Panadero等,2023年;Sparrow,2004年)。 内容
弱点是成本和其余的利率效应,并计入
只有在标题列出时或分级器离开时,可选择
这个

blocks.en:
P3 Closed formats. Multiple choice, classification and extraction
tasks are graded exactly and cheaply, which is why most legal NLP
benchmarks use them ( Chalkidis et al., 2022 ; Guha et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2020 ; Fei et al., 2024 ) .
But they measure a different construct. Law students gained from GPT-4
on multiple-choice questions but not on essays ( Choi and Schwarcz, 2025 ) ;
GPT-4’s bar exam percentile falls most on the essay component ( Martínez, 2025 ) .
blocks.zh:
P3 封闭格式。 多重选择、分类和提取
对任务进行精确和便宜的分级,这就是为什么大多数合法的NLP
使用基准(Chalkidis等,2022;Guha等,2023;Zhong等,2020;Fei等,2024)。
但是它们测量的是不同的构造。 从GPT-4获得的法学学生
关于多选择问题,但不关于散文(Choi和Schwarcz,2025年);
GPT-4的酒吧考试百分位数主要落在作文部分上(Martínez,2025年).

blocks.en:
P4 Similarity to a reference. Metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU and
BERTScore compare the answer with a reference text ( Lin, 2004 ; Papineni et al., 2002 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) . On legal
summaries, experts’ scores correlated with ROUGE at .13 to .21 and with
BERTScore at .07 ( Shukla et al., 2022 ) ; the model with the highest
ROUGE on case-law analyses produced the highest rate of unsupported
citations ( Hou et al., 2025 ) , and near-identical ROUGE on German court
press releases hid very different expert ranks ( Nagl et al., 2025 ) . Similarity can track grades within one
exam, where the reference is the expected solution: METEOR correlated
with the blind human grade on German case solutions at about .72 ( Nagl et al., 2026b ) . But it cannot give reasons, punishes a
defensible alternative path for using other words, and rewards copying
the reference.
blocks.zh:
P4与参考文献相似. 诸如Rouge、BLEU和
BERTSCore将答案与参考文本进行比较(Lin,2004;Papineni等,2002;Zhang等,2020.). 关于法律
13至21分,以及
BERTSCore at.07(Shukla等,2022年;型号最高).
关于判例法分析的ROUGE得出的无支持率最高
引用(Hou等人,2025年)和德国法院近乎相同的ROUGE
新闻稿隐藏了截然不同的专家队伍(Nagl等人,2025年)。 相似性可以追踪到一个内部的分数
测试,如果参考是预期的解决方案: 气象关系
与德国个案溶液上的盲人等级相差约.72分(Nagl等,2026b.). 但它不能给出理由,惩罚
使用其他词语的可辩护替代路径,以及复制奖励
参考文献。

blocks.en:
P5 LLM judge with a reference answer. The judge compares the
answer with a reference answer written by an expert, as in LEXam ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . Without a reference, judges agree with experts
only on questions they can answer themselves ( Krumdick et al., 2026 ) , and
judging accuracy tracks solving accuracy ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . With
a reference, LEXam’s judge passed the alternative annotator test against
three experts who agreed with each other at a quadratic weighted kappa
of .49 ( Calderon et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . A single reference
also fixes one path. In BenGER, the judge disagreed with human graders
most on presentation and on results reached by other reasoning paths
than the reference solution’s ( Nagl et al., 2026b ) , which is
exactly the answer latitude the law protects (L2). Such verdicts are
also judge-relative: in our earlier work, prompts optimized against a
strict judge on LEXam overfit to that judge’s disposition, while prompts
optimized against a lenient judge transferred better ( Elganayni et al., 2026 ) .

P5 LLM法官,有参考答复. 法官比较
如LEXam(Fan等人,2026年),用专家编写的参考答复回答。 没有参考文献,法官同意专家的意见
他们只能回答问题(Krumdick等人,2026年),以及
判断精度轨道解析精度(Tan等,2025年)。 与
LEXAM法官通过了针对

(Calderon等,2025;Fan等,2026)。 单一参考
也修正一条路径。 在BenGER, 法官不同意 人分级

(Nagl等人,2026年b),即
这正是法律所保护的答案纬度(L2)。 这些判决是:

blocks.en:
P6 LLM judge with generic criteria. The judge scores every answer
on the same generic dimensions ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . In law this fails
without task-specific guidance. Open models grading German criminal-law
case solutions without a sample solution or rubric reached correlations
near zero ( Wendlinger et al., 2024 ) , and a G-Eval-style
correctness judge, LeMAJ’s baseline (Table 3 ),
correlated with legal experts at .02 to .08 ( Enguehard et al., 2025 ) .
Generic dimensions combined with a reference fare better: BenGER’s
judge, which scores ten dimensions of German correction practice against
the reference solution, tracked the mean of blind human graders at r r = .76 with pass/fail κ \kappa = .60, inside the range of human
disagreement ( Nagl et al., 2026b ) , and a judge with general
criteria ranked systems for German court press releases much as experts
did ( Nagl et al., 2025 ) . What makes such judges work is the
task-specific content they receive (P7).

blocks.en:
P7 LLM judge with an instance-specific rubric. An expert writes,
for each task, the criteria an answer must meet, often as atomic
yes-or-no items, and the judge checks each criterion. Outside law, this
design gives judges high agreement with experts per criterion. On
HealthBench’s 34 consensus criteria, GPT-4.1 agreed with physicians at a
macro-F1 of .71, where the average physician scored .57 to .73 by theme ( Arora et al., 2025 ) , with similar judge agreement on rubric
trees for research replication and on expert rubrics in science, finance
and consulting ( Starace et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ;
controlled comparisons favour instance-specific criteria over general
ones, over a plain prompt and over free grading ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) .
In law, the within-domain comparisons point the same way, with caveats.
On German exams, GPT-5 with a sample solution and a grading scheme
reached a quadratic weighted kappa of .60 in criminal and .91 in public
law, against .31 and .58 with neither; the scheme alone gave most of the
gain (.56 and .85), the solution alone less (.39 and .79) ( Al Zubaer et al., 2026 ) . The gain is not universal: for GPT-5.1 the
same additions lowered agreement, and the two sets are 71 take-home
solutions and 16 timed mock-exam scripts reused from earlier studies ( Wendlinger et al., 2024 ; Strecker et al., 2026 ) . On four US law-school
finals with 205 scripts, GPT-5 with the professor’s rubric correlated
with the professor’s grades at .78 to .93, mean .87, against .66 to .80
with a bare prompt; forcing a score per rubric element changed little
(mean .87, better on two exams and worse on two), and pairwise
comparison with the rubric reached a mean of .86 ( Cope et al., 2026 ) ; on the one question a professor regraded, the
two human gradings agreed more with each other than either did with the
model, a gap the authors do not find significant. On attorney-written
binary rubrics for legal research, judges from three providers agreed
with the attorneys’ majority label at κ \kappa = .71 to .73, against a
human baseline of .64 that the authors report as attorney-to-attorney
agreement, a different comparison ( Drozdov et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
The weaknesses are real. Expert rubrics cost time: building each
PLawBench item, rubric included, took about three expert hours ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Generated rubrics fall short of expert ones ( Wang and Blanco, 2026 ; Dhole and Agichtein, 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , and
LLM-written elaborations of human rubrics lowered agreement ( Sharma et al., 2025 ) . Finer label schemes lower agreement:
moving from a binary to a five-way label scheme on short science answers
cut accuracy from 76% to 57% ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and binary
grading of the same criteria agreed with humans about 20 points better
than ternary grading ( Sharma et al., 2025 ) . A related
finding comes from reference-based judges under a generic grading
regulation: where the regulation was silent, 22 of 26 LLM judges scored
in or near the majority reading of three examiners and none reproduced
the defensible minority one, a dissent among graders about the same
answer rather than an alternative path taken by the candidate ( Akarajaradwong et al., 2026 ) . Even a judge given the committee’s
criteria and the correct legal analysis gave 85 to 90 of 100 points to
three written judgments that the committee had failed for serious
errors, where the committee gave 8 to 37 ( Karp et al., 2025 ) . And
grading against a rubric invites manipulation: instructions embedded in
an answer succeeded in 56.9% of attacks on average across rubric-based
graders ( Li et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
P8 Pairwise comparison. The grader compares two answers and picks
the better one; many comparisons yield a ranking, as in Chatbot Arena ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) or comparative judgment. The strongest
counter-evidence to rubrics comes from this paradigm. In JudgmentBench,
practising attorneys graded answers to 30 BigLaw Bench tasks at three
quality levels: their pairwise judgments recovered the order of the
levels with a mean Spearman’s ρ \rho of .91, their rubric scores only
with .15, and the rubric raters agreed with each other at .44; a GPT-5.4
autograder tracked the attorneys’ orderings at .38 with pairwise
judgments and .20 with the rubric ( Yang et al., 2026 ) .
Pairwise ranking also beat absolute scoring for essays ( Shibata and Miyamura, 2025 ) and resisted universal adversarial phrases
better ( Raina et al., 2024 ) . The quality levels in JudgmentBench were
induced by prompting and moved all dimensions together, and the rubrics
were not validated against graded answers; real answers differ in which
issues they treat, which is what rubrics capture. Pairwise judges show
position and length bias ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Dubois et al., 2024 ) . Above
all, a bare preference is relative: it ranks a script among others but
gives no criterion-referenced reasons, no feedback, and no grade that
holds when the cohort changes. That conflicts with the duty to give
reasons (L3) and with criterion-referenced grading, towards which even
the bar exam is moving ( Light et al., 2024 ) . The objection is to the
protocol, not to comparison as such: a pairwise judge with the rubric
matched absolute rubric grading on US exams ( Cope et al., 2026 ) , and
anchored comparisons with a reason per criterion are untested. As used
today, P8 suits leaderboards better than exams.

blocks.en:
The field has moved from P3 and P4 to P7. Legal benchmarks long
reduced law to closed formats or scored generation with overlap or
keyword metrics ( Chalkidis et al., 2022 ; Fei et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025b ) .
Since 2025, the leading benchmarks and the practitioners’ own
evaluations have adopted instance-specific rubrics, written or seeded by
experts, with an LLM judge ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ; Drozdov et al., 2026 ; Grupen et al., 2026 ; Vals AI and Legaltech Hub, 2025 ) .
blocks.zh:
外地已从P3和P4改为P7。 法律基准长度
将定律简化为封闭格式或有重叠的分数生成或
关键词衡量标准(Charkidis等,2022;Fei等,2024;Li等,2024;Li等,2025b)。
自2025年以来,主要基准和从业人员
评价采用了特定实例标题,由作者编写或制作。
专家,有LLM法官(Shi等,2026;Chen等,2026;Oh等,2026;Drozdov等,2026;Grupen等,2026;Vals AI和Legaltech Hub,2025)。

blocks.en:
Task-specific content is the strongest lever, within limits. Within the same domain, a scheme or rubric raised the agreement of the
same model, a score per rubric element and pairwise comparison added
nothing further, the gain varies by model, and the two German sets reuse
the scripts of earlier studies (Section 5 ).
Decomposition can also start from the answer instead of the expected
performance: LeMAJ splits a model’s answer into legal data points and
checks each against the source material without a reference answer ( Enguehard et al., 2025 ) . The two are not the same: a rubric states in
advance what counts as performance and who answers for it, while answer
decomposition structures the checking, omissions included, and supplies
neither the weights nor the grade.
blocks.zh:
针对具体任务的内容是极限内最有力的杠杆。 在同一领域,一个计划或标题提出了该企业的协议。
同一型号,每个分数和双相比较
没有什么进一步,收益因型号而异, 两个德国套装再利用

blocks.en:
Validation is often thin, and human-level claims depend on the
unit of comparison. Several rubric benchmarks report agreement between
judges but not with humans ( Pires et al., 2026 ) , validate on
three candidate scripts that all passed ( Pires et al., 2025 ) , or
publish no agreement at all ( Harvey Team, 2024 ; Grupen et al., 2026 ) . Agreement between judges
is not validity ( Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026 ; Han and Kim, 2026 ) . Few studies report
the agreement of their human graders, and where both are reported the
comparison is rarely like for like: judges are scored against a majority
or a mean while humans are scored against each other ( Drozdov et al., 2026 ; Chlapanis et al., 2025 ; Nagl et al., 2026b ) ,
the alternative annotator test being the exception (S5), a panel of
three judges agrees with itself better than three examiners agree with
each other, without this showing that it agrees with them ( Akarajaradwong et al., 2026 ) , and the sharpest contrasts come from
constructed quality levels ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Correlation is
not accuracy: a correlation of one is compatible with every grade three
points too high, harmless for a ranking and decisive for pass or fail.

What earns credit. Graders of law essays reward the treatment of
major issues more than minor ones ( Linn et al., 1972 ) , and a correct
result without the authority behind it is a different achievement from a
correct, authority-grounded answer ( Liao, 2026 ) . A rubric
that credits bare results penalizes defensible alternatives and rewards
guessing; one that credits the reasoning (the requirement stated, the
facts subsumed and the argument weighed) fits both legal method and the
answer latitude (L2).

blocks.en:
Granularity and scale. Yes-or-no verdicts agree better than
partial-credit or finer label schemes ( Sharma et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) , and on binary expert
criteria, experts agree almost perfectly ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . But
splitting further does not always help ( Kortemeyer et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Agreement is not the
construct: coarser labels raise agreement partly by discarding
information. The granularity should follow what the step tests, in units
a grader can judge without ambiguity, and the states not met , not applicable , uncertain and check failed must
stay apart even where the criterion is binary. The middle ground is a
step for each expected legal performance, with a few binary requirements
per step; on US exams the most granular rubric, not the most granular
output, gave the highest agreement, a hypothesis from four exams ( Cope et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Structure and weights. German point schemes come in three types.
In the first, every point belongs to a step of the expected solution,
either as absolute points per step ( Heidebach, 2015 ; Frenzel, 2011 ) or as a percentage of
the total for each item of the outline, so that no conversion key is
needed ( Strecker et al., 2026 , pp. 12 f.) . In the second, a fixed share
goes to steps and a pool is bound to named criteria, typically method
points ( Strukturpunkte ) for structure, appraisal style and
language, for which 15 to 25% is proposed ( Strecker et al., 2026 , p. 14) ; the same criteria can instead be credited
within each section, the option we propose. In the third, the pool is
free: the grader distributes it on an overall impression. A free pool is
tied to nothing a second grader or a model could check and reintroduces
the variance the sheet was meant to remove, so it has no place in a
rubric judge; a criteria-bound pool is checkable as far as its criteria
are stated and its share is fixed. A bounded overall component that must
name what it rewards, such as the weighting of issues or an unforeseen
but sound solution, can be stated, limited and reviewed, and belongs in
the design space as a documented hybrid (Section 10 ).

blocks.en:
Alternatives and follow-on errors. Where a dispute changes only a
result or its reasons, a criterion can credit the argument whatever the
result. Where another defensible decision removes or adds steps, the
rubric needs a separate path whose steps are weighted for equal
performance, not for equal length, and answers that take a path no one
foresaw should go to the examiner. A worked example shows the three
cases a rubric must keep apart. Suppose question A decides whether step
B is reached. If the candidate denies A defensibly, B falls away and
neither earns nor loses points, unless the task asks for an auxiliary
opinion ( Hilfsgutachten ), in which case B is still expected. If
the candidate denies A wrongly, what follows from that decision is a
follow-on error, judged against the candidate’s own decision with the
weight of the wrong decision left to the examiner, while a new error
inside B counts on its own. The rubric must therefore record why a step
is absent, or it credits work not shown, or penalizes a lawful path for
omitting steps it did not need; and a judge must not pick, from a
contradictory answer, the path that scores best. Marking B as not
applicable does not settle the total: if A carries four points and B
six, a denominator of ten penalizes the lawful path, and rescaling to
four turns a shorter performance into a full score. Alternative paths
need a rule, set by the examiner, for comparable scoring opportunities
and for the total.

Who writes the rubric, and when. The examiner sets the standard
(L4). The rubric is fixed before grading; a defect found while grading
is corrected in a new version, the change is documented, and every
script graded under the old version is regraded on the changed criteria
(L1). A model can draft the rubric, but drafting is more than extracting
the reference solution: the solution does not say which steps earn which
points, what can be expected under exam conditions, which alternatives
are equal or which errors weigh most. A draft should mark, per
criterion, whether it restates the task, the solution or the examiner’s
notes, adds an alternative, proposes a weight or assumes something the
examiner must confirm, and the examiner must review and adopt it
(Section 10 ).

blocks.en:
Table 2 shows no paradigm without weaknesses. P7 leads
on validity, reasons and scale, but it is open to manipulation, its
reliability is not guaranteed, and whether it credits alternatives or
improves learning is untested. We call a rubric judge trustworthy when safeguards close these gaps far enough for the intended use, and we
propose seven. Each has support in the literature, from law or from
other domains; the combination is new, and Section 10 states
the tests it must pass. Most safeguards would also fit a reference-based
or pairwise judge, but only a rubric makes every reason checkable
against a criterion. RULERS is the closest prior design outside law ( Hong et al., 2026 ) ; what is specific here is the legal standard,
with alternative paths, follow-on errors, examiner-set weights and the
examiner’s decision. Figure 1 shows the design.

The rubric and the examiner are human, the judge is a model, the quote check and the total are code, and the dashed box is a procedure of code and humans run before use. S1 An instance rubric of atomic criteria that credits
arguments. Experts write, or review, criteria for each task that state
the performance an answer must show ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Drozdov et al., 2026 ) . To respect
the answer latitude (L2), criteria credit arguments, alternatives get
paths of their own, and follow-on errors are judged on the candidate’s
own decisions (Section 7 ). Where a model drafts the
rubric, an expert must review it, since generated rubrics fall short of
expert ones ( Wang and Blanco, 2026 ; Dhole and Agichtein, 2026 ) . The rubric
is fixed before grading; a correction creates a new version that is
applied to every script (L1). The rubric’s weights are set by the
examiner, and the arithmetic is done by code, because LLMs make mistakes
when they add numbers ( Kortemeyer et al., 2024 ) . No legal grader has
yet been probed with alternative paths or follow-on errors; S3 makes
both a standard probe.

never a deduction. The quote gives the examiner and the candidate the

S3 Probes before use. Before grading real answers, a judge and
rubric must pass answers with known outcomes. Fake answers come first:
empty and off-topic answers and copies of the fact pattern must score
near zero, the reference solution must score high, and an answer with
embedded instructions must not gain. Controlled variants of one real
answer come second, each with its permitted change in score fixed in
advance: irrelevant padding must not raise the score, a paraphrase that
keeps the legal performance must not change it, a defensible alternative
path must keep its credit, the removal of a decisive reason must lose
it, and an appended instruction must change nothing. A follow-on error
probe changes an upstream decision and keeps later steps consistent with
it: the score may change only as the examiner’s dependency rule says,
and a new error inside a dependent step must still be found. Known
attacks give the probe set ( Raina et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Milani et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) ;
probes answer the AI Act’s demand for robustness (L6) but show only that

S4 Repeated runs and variance decomposition. A judge grades the
same answer differently on another run ( Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025 ; Schroeder and Wood-Doughty, 2024 ) . Generalizability theory
separates sources of error such as runs, judges and rubrics ( Brennan, 2001 ) , has been applied to LLM raters ( Song et al., 2026 ) , and the rubric facet matters most where
rubrics are generated: a poor rubric can make every grade consistent by
forcing the same error on every script, so less spread is not success.
Stability within a rubric, differences between rubrics, systematic
severity and consequential errors must be reported apart, as equal
standards (L1) and the AI Act’s accuracy duty (L6) require. High
self-consistency does not prove validity ( Norman et al., 2026 ; Sunkavalli, 2026 ) , so S4 complements S5
and does not replace it.

blocks.en:
S5 Calibration against independent human grades. The judge is
validated on a sample of answers graded blind and independently by
humans, and its agreement is read against the agreement among the
humans, for instance with the alternative annotator test ( Calderon et al., 2025 ; Nagl et al., 2026b ) . The human grades
must be independent, since second graders who see the first grade agree
more ( Vidal Rodeiro, 2007 ) . And where several grades are
defensible, validation should accept a set of grades rather than one:
judges selected against forced single labels performed up to 31% worse ( Guerdan et al., 2025 ) . Calibration and the final test must use
different data, split by task rather than by script if the claim is
about new exams. Calibration must be repeated when the model changes:
model updates shifted judge severity by up to 133 of 1,000 points ( Sunkavalli, 2026 ) . Calibration must also keep improvements in
criterion application apart from changes to the standard: a learned
transformation of criterion weights or of the point-to-grade mapping,
such as the regression onto human scores in RULERS ( Hong et al., 2026 ) , is a grading decision in its own right and must
be reviewed and adopted by the examiner (L4).

S6 Escalation to the examiner. The judge proposes, and the
examiner decides (L4, L5). For a graded exam the examiner must read
every script personally ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2002 ) , so unflagged scripts
are not waved through. Flags are not only confidence: answers on
unforeseen paths, contradictions in the answer, criteria the judge could
not apply, failed quote checks, zeroed credits and grades near the pass
mark go to the examiner whatever its confidence, since a confidently
wrong grade is the failure that matters. Where the judge is uncertain,
it abstains; selective evaluation can guarantee a chosen level of human
agreement on the retained cases ( Jung et al., 2025 ) or raise it
empirically ( Kortemeyer and Nöhl, 2025 ) , an average that says
nothing about one candidate. Since second readers are drawn towards a
grade they have seen ( Vidal Rodeiro, 2007 ) , the examiner
should form a view before seeing the model’s grade. This is a method,
not a legal duty: federal constitutional law does not forbid open second
correction ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2002 ) . Whether examiners catch a
confidently wrong proposal is the test this safeguard must pass
(Section 10 ).

S7 Documentation and data protection. Every grade records the
rubric version, judge, model version, prompts, quotes and checks behind
it, the judge’s original proposal and every human change with its
reason, kept apart as a corrected criterion application, a rubric change
or a reasoned individual decision. This is the logging and transparency
the AI Act requires (L6) and what a candidate may request where the
grade is an automated decision ( Court of Justice of the European Union, 2025 ) .
Pseudonymized scripts and local models are building blocks, not a data
protection concept: the controller, the legal basis, access rights and
retention, deletion, and any external service each need a decision of
their own (L7).

The safeguards have costs. Under strict quality targets the savings can
be modest: in one calculus exam, about 70% of items had to go to humans
to reach human accuracy ( Kortemeyer et al., 2025 ) . A trustworthy
rubric judge therefore assists human graders; it does not replace them.

blocks.zh: 9. 国家 证据支持什么

blocks.en:
The uses differ in stakes and in who bears an error, so the evidence
supports them unequally.

blocks.en:
Formative feedback. Feedback on practice exams is where the case
is strongest. Rubric use and feedback improve learning ( Panadero et al., 2023 ; Wisniewski et al., 2020 ) , individual feedback
raised law students’ grades ( Schwarcz and Farganis, 2017 ) , and the American
Bar Association (ABA) now requires a formative assessment in every
course of the first third of the J.D. ( American Bar Association, Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar, 2026 ) . A rubric
judge can return, for each criterion, what was met, the passage that met
it and what was missing. Whether model-written feedback improves
learning in law is untested; students in German law still tended to
prefer tutor feedback ( Hackl et al., 2024 ) , and generous model
grades mislead, so feedback should state its uncertainty.

A second reader in graded exams. A rubric judge that flags
scripts where its total and the examiner’s differ is plausible, and a
review of the largest discrepancies on US exams found errors by the
professor as well as by the model ( Cope et al., 2026 ) , but it is
barely tested. German law requires the examiner to decide (L4). Since
the features of the procedure that shape the result, such as the number
of examiners and the handling of their differences, must be fixed by
rule ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2019 , paras. 15 to 17) , we argue that a
machine role that shapes the assessment belongs in the exam regulations
too, as pre-marking by assistants is admissible only where the procedure
provides for it ( Bundesverwaltungsgericht, 2002 ) .

blocks.en: 10. Open problems
blocks.zh: 10个 打开问题

blocks.en:
Who writes the rubric, and how is a generated one judged? Expert
rubrics are the bottleneck. Generating them from the reference solution
is the obvious step, but generated rubrics fell short of expert ones in
the comparisons made so far, which generated them without a reference
solution ( Wang and Blanco, 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , the one legal
set generated from expert solutions was only partly reviewed ( Oh et al., 2026 ) , and whether expert review can close the gap at
acceptable cost is open; rubrics refined against human-scored answers
matched detailed human-written ones in essay scoring ( Harada et al., 2025 ) , a route to which the caveat of S5 applies.
A study of generated legal rubrics must validate three objects apart:
the rubric as an instrument, its application to real scripts, and the
whole workflow with the examiner in it. It needs serious comparators (an
independent expert sheet, rubrics generated in one pass and step by
step, the same after expert revision, and a reference-based judge
without rubric), a split by task rather than by script, the expert sheet
as a reference instrument rather than the only right answer, so that
deviations are classified before they count as errors, and endpoints
beyond correlation: wrong passes and fails, criterion errors,
alternatives and follow-on errors, robustness to the probes of S3 and
the examiner’s time. Our companion study on German exams starts this
programme with generated sheets, their application, and an examiner’s
sheet as the reference ( Nagl et al., 2026a ) .

Holistic quality. Some legal quality, such as weighing, judgment
and persuasiveness, may resist criteria fixed in advance ( Sadler, 2009 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Hybrids that add
a bounded, reasoned overall component or a pairwise component to
criterion checks (Section 7 ) and document each share need

blocks.en:
The human reference. Judges are calibrated against human graders
who disagree with each other and carry their own biases ( Hufeld, 2024 ; Towfigh et al., 2018 ) . Matching them is a low bar,
and matching their majority can silence a defensible minority reading ( Akarajaradwong et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:

the rubric rather than the law, as prompts optimized against a judge
learn its disposition ( Elganayni et al., 2026 ) ; whether skill or
only scores improve is open.

11. Limitations
blocks.zh: 11. 限制

blocks.en:
Our search is structured but not exhaustive, and several of the most
relevant studies are 2026 preprints. The ratings in Table 2 are one author’s reading of uneven evidence, much of
it from outside law. Several entries in Table 3 share
data or instruments (marked reused ) and BenGER is our own, so the
number of papers overstates the number of independent confirmations.
German law is the worked example, and other jurisdictions constrain
grading differently. Five cited works are our own, one of them in
preparation ( Nagl et al., 2026b ; Nagl and Grabmair, 2026 ; Nagl et al., 2025 ; Elganayni et al., 2026 ; Nagl et al., 2026a ) ,
and the author works on rubric judges, which may bias the reading
towards them; we have tried to ask the same questions of every study.

blocks.en: 12. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 12. 结论

blocks.en:
The evidence from law, education and NLP shows that a rubric written for
the task is the strongest lever for agreement with human graders, and
examination law shows why rubric-centred grading is the family worth
building on: it makes the standard explicit, its application contestable
and the decision the examiner’s. What the evidence does not yet show is
that any judge credits defensible alternatives, counts a follow-on error
once, resists manipulation, or is corrected by examiners when it is
confidently wrong. The trustworthy rubric judge is our answer to these
gaps: seven safeguards, each tied to a legal requirement, and a test
programme for what is not yet shown. Today it is best placed for
feedback and benchmarks, and as an assistant, not a replacement, where
grades count.
